utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber regrets that we had a late start although not as late as the clock in the courtroom tells. We'll start with giving an opportunity to the Prosecution to respond to -- to reply to the responses given by the Defence on the 54 bis motion. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Always dangerous to say I will try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not -- it is encouraging.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fundamentally, Your Honours, the Rule 54 bis application is a matter between the Prosecution and the state of Croatia. The prosecution's obligation is to demonstrate to the Chamber under the terms of Rule 54 bis that it has taken reasonable step to obtain documents from the Croatian authorities that are relevant and important to its case. The Prosecution has met this burden. Indeed, the Defence challenges have not asserted that the steps taken by the Prosecution were insufficient to warrant a Rule 54 bis order nor have they challenged the importance or relevance of the documents. Indeed their response itself impliedly acknowledges that the motion is well founded and that the necessary steps have indeed been taken. Instead rather than focussing on the reasonable steps requirement of Rule 54 bis which has been fulfilled, the Defence attempts to introduce Rule 65, and focus on the timing of the application. In fact, Your Honour, there is no overlap between the two. The issue of the introduction of documents is a separate matter, no prejudice results from the Prosecution's attempt to obtain documents, and if and when such documents are obtained, if and when the Prosecution seeks to introduce those documents either in the context of an expert report or otherwise, the Trial Chamber will be in a position to assess the propriety of introducing those documents in the context of both what occurred and the particular documents involved. Now, the Defence in part attempts to overcome the problem that Rule 54 bis is not the same as Rule 65 by mischaracterizing exchanges with the Pre-Trial Chamber during pre-trial proceedings. In fact no instructions were issued by the Pre-Trial Chamber to the Prosecution to do any particular thing. The issue of the possibility of assistance from the Pre-Trial Chamber arose in the context of the Prosecution's attempts to gain access to the archives before July of 2007, by -- that was a concrete problem with -- to which the Pre-Trial Chamber might have been able to direct its attention and the Prosecution alerted the Pre-Trial Chamber to that possibility by July of 2007, when the Court sees some citations to the pre-trial conference and the 65 ter, the Prosecution had managed to overcome that particular problem and then new issues arose, in particular the question of having gained access to the archives and having scoured the archives and continuing in its determination to make sure that those documents were not there as represented by Croatian authorities. Then the Prosecution continued to work with Croatian authorities as they claimed that they were attempting to locate documents that were purportedly not in the archives and certainly not accessible based on the Prosecution's review. It was when the convergence of information revealed that those steps, though efforts to work cooperatively with the Republic of Croatia as mandated but Rule 54 bis were not successful and not only were the efforts an investigations of the Croatian authorities yielding negligible result but further information revealed that the same persons previously involved in efforts to secret or conceal documents from the OTP had now been engaged in the purported effort to locate the documents that were purportedly not in the archives that the Prosecution move forward on the basis of the fact that those cooperative efforts were not going to yield the appropriate results. Further, Your Honour, let me note that in addition to what I have indicated is a mischaracterisation of the events at the time of the pre-trial conference, there is no basis whatsoever for the allegation by the Defence that the Prosecution deliberately delayed the filing of the 54 bis in order to affect the outcome of the Gotovina motion to strike, apart from the fact that that was a procedural motion which was not dependant upon any kind of factual basis in any event, the Defence motions themselves reveal that the Defence and the Court was fully aware of the fact that the Prosecution was looking for a large number of documents related to artillery, and one merely needs to look at the October 2007 65 ter conference at page 141 in addition to the citations offered by the Defence themselves to realise that and I say again that that allegation is baseless, unfounded, and is categorically rejected. Finally, Your Honour, with respect to the issue of documents allegedly object obtained in violation of the rules, I will emphasise these documents are not covered by Rule 70 or Rule 54 bis (F) and with that I would like to move quickly into private session to more fully address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, in response to Mr. Tieger's presentation let me say that I believe that is a mischaracterisation of what their obligations under Rule 354 bis in order to obtain the order. This whole situation basically amounts to what is fair and what is happening here is fundamentally unfair to the defendants, in particular to my client, General Gotovina, in light of the extensive discussions, conversations with the Trial Chamber prior to trial specifically at Rule 65 ter conferences and at Status Conference regarding the need to ensure that the rights of the accused were properly taken care of prior to trial, combined with the Prosecution's need to obtain relevant documents prior to trial. I need only cite you to Mr. Tieger's own words about the need to balance these efforts at the 6 July 2007 Status Conference, at page 249, and in an exchange with Judge Moloto, when Mr. Tieger pledged, and I quote: "Now when we come to a point that begins to implicate the commencement of trial the Defence's ability to prepare and deal with documents that we'll be submitting, then we have to impose a deadline irrespective of the success of these efforts," and I should say we may be asking the Court at some point to assist with those efforts if they're not successful. At this point, we're pursuing them as vigorously as we can. Judge Moloto then says: "When you talk of imposing a deadline, imposing it on who, on the archival sources or on --" Mr. Tieger then says: "On ourselves for the preparation and submission of those calling it a deadline for the submission of those reports." So, the linkage between their efforts with the archival source, their need to prepare expert reports, the commencement of the trial date and the Defence's ability to prepare and deal with their documents, all were the subject of extensive conversation, discussion with both the Defence and the Pre-Trial Judge. Now, what this amounts to or what this boils down to is what is fair in this situation. Rule 54 bis in addition to imposing the step which Mr. Tieger referred to in his presentation under Rule 54 bis (B) (ii) about taking reasonable steps, the first problem that they have to -- the first hurdle that they have to clear says Rule 54 bis (B)(i) that the documents they seek or information -- I'm sorry. Let me read the whole rule: "The judge the Trial Chamber or may reject an application under paragraph A in limine if in satisfied that, one, the documents or information are not relevant to any matter in issue in the proceedings before them or are not necessary for a fair determination of any such matter." Now there in the rule, the matter of fairness is inserted and can be considered and should be considered by the Trial Chamber before issuing an order under Rule 54 bis and fairness, is precisely what our response deals with. So the Trial Chamber in fact at this stage should consider whether these documents ultimately would be admissible or would be necessary for the Trial Chamber or would be fair to admit. It is our submission, Your Honours, that not only are these documents not necessary for a fair determination, it goes beyond that. The use of these document would say be fundamentally unfair, in light of the Prosecution's own failures not only I would say to act with due diligence, but this was a conscious thought-out considered decision by the Prosecution not to take up the Trial Chamber's offer from July and October to assist them in obtaining these documents. This is not a situation where the Prosecution has discovered new evidence or discovered the existence of evidence in the middle of trial. This is a situation where and even at the July 2007 conference, if I may speak for the Defence, Mr. Kehoe said if you need the documents, then we would just urge you to go ahead and ask the Trial Chamber for assistance now but please, please, please, please, don't do it on the eve of trial and implicitly don't do it during trial so that the Defence is disadvantaged. Our position, Your Honour, is that now, as a result of the Prosecution's conscious willing thought-out decision to not raise this issue for a year, to wait until the middle of trial to do this, all of the negative consequences of this action is being proposed to be shifted on to the defendants. That is fundamentally unfair. The Prosecution, and let me start it off by saying we are assuming for the purposes of this motion that these documents even exist. But let's say they do exist. It is now the Prosecution's implied position that any negative consequences as a result of their own dilatory conduct are now the defendant's burdens to bear. That is not fair. With respect to the assertion in Mr. Tieger' argument that they took reasonable steps I think our position on the papers is quite the opposite. I believe that the reasonable steps that should have been taken were clearly spelled out in July and in October. That reasonable step was to move then before the commencement of trial to seek the Trial Chamber's assistance. The Prosecution from the Prosecution apparently now is is that having failed to do what was reasonable a year ago, they start with a clean slate and now we can start as if this issue has suddenly appeared and we can go into the matter again, without having to refer back to their failure to take the reasonable step from before. With respect to -- and I'm not sure I understood the argument but there was some I think attempts to say that what we were discussing in July is not related to what we're discussing today. I think that, quite frankly is contradicted by the Prosecution's own motion. One only need to look at the fact that the document request they are seeking assistance on was issued in November 2006. So apparently this was what was discussed in July of 2007 and in October of 2007. They know it and they know they failed to take steps on this. Whatever was going on behind the scenes, it seems quite clear and Judge Moloto made it quite clear that they needed to move prior to trial to seek the Trial Chamber's assistance. They failed to do so. Your Honour, if I may, how much time do I have left? I didn't mark the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. I'm not -- I don't believe we're mischaracterizing any of the exchanges is what Mr. Tieger suggests. I think the record is quite clear and the Trial Chamber needs only to review the transcripts of what was being discussed. Our point was quite simple: Let us have a fair opportunity to meet the Prosecution's case. I have already quoted Mr. Tieger as having acknowledged that to be fair to the defendants, this needed to be taken care of prior to trial. Now I can only look at the Prosecution's shelling expert report and say that apparently the Prosecution felt that that was, to them, simply an early draft of the report that they intended or intend to submit, because, at the same time that they're submitting an expert report on shelling, they're also pursuing apparently several hundred categories of documents on shelling. They don't alert the Trial Chamber to this fact, they don't alert the defendants to this fact and now presumably we're going to get -- after a Rule 54 bis order is issued they want to then submit a final report which will be I'm certain much different than the report that is currently filed with the register. This is fundamental unfairness and the defendant should not be made to bear the burden of the Prosecution's own decisions prior to trial to essentially reject the Pre-Trial Judge offer to seek the Trial Chamber's assistance. We still have not heard a rational explanation of why this was not taken care of last year. I waited for Mr. Tieger to provide that explanation. I still fail to understand in light of the importance to the Prosecution's case of the artillery allegation in light of the fact that this Trial Chamber has heard now three months of evidence on artillery, it is clearly a pillar of the Prosecution's case that we still have not heard a rational explanation of why this was not handled before or why the Prosecution decided not to seek the Trial Chamber's assistance. With respect to the remaining parts of Mr. Tieger's presentation, I am quite frankly surprised that the Prosecution takes the position that communications -- well, let me take a step back. The document at issue was indeed not authored by the Defence. It was my understanding based on practice that communications of one party and a Rule 70 provider were confidential. The Prosecution is now taking a contrary position and therefore I assume is of the position that the defendants have free reign now to discover all their communications with Rule 70 providers. I don't think that is their position and I don't think a double standard should be imposed on us. To the extent that there is implication that and, I think I read between the lines, Mr. Tieger implying that the Croatian government itself is secreting documents, I found nothing in the Prosecution's papers s to suggest that. Indeed the assertion that the Croatian government since March 1996 is secreting documents that the Prosecution didn't even think to ask for until November 2006 borders on the absurd. And then the subimplication that the Gotovina Defence is secreting documents from the Prosecution is an allegation that requires a bit more proof than was given by Mr. Tieger there and I can say without any hesitation that that is -- that implication is categorically false and disappointing to hear. In short, Your Honour, and in conclusion, again, to me and to us, this boils down to simply a question of fairness. The question of fairness is something you can consider under Rule 54 bis as I cited. We would ask that the Trial Chamber consider that, consider whether it would be fair ultimately to admit these documents and in the absence of any coherent explanation from the Prosecution as to why this -- these issues were not addressed prior to trial, I would ask the Trial Chamber to reject the Rule 54 bis application. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. You also stayed well within the time allocated to you. One of the things that puzzles me in your submissions is that you're talking about a Rule 70 provider. I always understood Rule 70 to be that certain information or documents are provided under Rule 70, which, of course in relation to that material makes the provider a Rule 70 provider, but it seems that you have a broader concept of what the rules are if material is provided by a provider who has previously or at other instances invoked Rule 70 protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would require a bit more briefing, but I think I can cite, if given the opportunity or if the Trial Chamber wants the citations there is prior Tribunal jurisprudence which analogises the Rule 70 (A) provisions to what is known in the United States and I believe in the UK as the work product doctrine. I believe that the work product doctrine, if in fact the Tribunal's jurisprudence can be ready to say that Rule 70 actually is more akin to the work product doctrine, communications between a party and what we refer to as a third-party provider, although not technically a representative, would be confidential, both in the request that is submitted to the third-party provider and the -- any internal memoranda created by the third-party provider to comply with the request that was issued. Now, as I said, as a matter of practice, it was and would have been and has been, to me, up to this point, inconceivable that we would ask, for example to issue a document request to the Republic of Croatia saying, Please give us all of your communications with the Office of the Prosecutor. It simply would be fundamentally unfair and I believe that the parties at the very least up until now have been operating under the assumption that parties should be able to have communications with a third-party provider that are not discoverable by the other side because I think that inherently then impedes both sides, because our theory of the case, what avenues we're pursuing, what avenues they're pursuing can be deciphered from communications as to what it is that we're interested in or what it is that they're interested in. So, as it strictly -- on its face, you are you correct, we would assert that the Republic of Croatia is a representative of the Defence, as I don't think they are a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. But up until this point we have I think not just in this case but I'm pretty sure, and the other counsel can speak to the other cases that they have appeared in before this Tribunal, that requests for communications with the other side by a third party is not something that generally has been done at this Tribunal and it is for that reason that this situation we believe has gone outside of the norm here and I believe would be outside what has generally been interpreted as the work product doctrine thus far of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which raises the issue the Chamber has no idea where these documents come from. I don't know whether we can deal with it in open session or not. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These documents -- well, we don't either so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless you invoke that this is the result of a kind of a protected communications with the -- but perhaps before we continue here we move into private session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I think we then are at a point to ask the Prosecution whether it's ready to call its next witness. Mr. Du Toit, is it you who is going to take that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And if we could just a moment just to switch positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Du Toit, I think there was one issue of the status of an information sheet, which I think you communicated to the Chamber's legal officer that you would seek guidance. MR. DU TOIT: That is indeed so, Mr. President. And the appropriate time might be at a certain stage where the certain document is dealt with and my intention is to, especially the one orientation map will be dealt with sort at the end of the witness testimony and maybe at that time it would be appropriate for me to request the Court some guidance. The one other matter is, as you probably have also seen, Mr. President, is that these two statements that the witness made that is not -- was not part of the 92 ter motion itself, these two statements is referred to in one of the statements of the witness, the one on 18 July 2007, in specific paragraph 2 is mention of a statement that the witness made on the 10th of March in 1996 and in paragraph 43 of the 18 July 2007 statement there's also reference of another statement that the witness made in August 1995, and I will request the Court to allow me from the bar table to also refer to these two statements. As I say, I have uploaded them into e-court. They have been provided provisional 65 ter numbers and I will request at the appropriate time to be permitted to add them to the 65 ter exhibit list and also to deal with the witness. I have informed the Defence about that also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Steenbergen. I suppose. Yes. I didn't see you come into the courtroom. We were dealing with a procedural matter. I apologise for that. Mr. Steenbergen, before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. I see that your microphones are not switched on. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Mr. Steenbergen, I addressed you in English, not in Dutch since we have no interpretation. Whenever you feel uncomfortable either by understanding what is asked or in expressing yourself in answering questions, you may address me, not to say that we will then continue in Dutch but at least we're aware there is a problem. Mr. Du Toit, are you ready? MR. DU TOIT: I'm ready. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Du Toit:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Steenbergen. Can you state your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: My name is Herman Steenbergen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you state your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: At this moment I am a medical inspector at DUD medical department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have the rank of colonel, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: The rank of lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Steenbergen, is it correct that over the weekend we meet and we dealt with various statements that you made on various times with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the first one I want to deal with you is your witness statement that you made to the office dated the 18th of July, 2007. MR. DU TOIT: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could maybe please call that up, it is 65 ter 05236, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, in front of you is that statement. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: I recognise this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your conversation you also provided certain additional information and informed me that you wanted to correct a few aspects of this statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. Registrar, can we move please to page 5 of that statement, paragraph 32, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, the second line of that paragraph reads: "During this second period of shelling we received an evacuation order for Knin HQ?" Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. From, must be from the HQ. MR. DU TOIT: Can we move, please, to page 6, paragraph 40, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last line, you indicated: "During the afternoon of the 4th of August we observed Croatian troops by JorBat 3 camp." Now, did you observe any troops in fact on the 4th, or was that also a mistake?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: It must be on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I will also deal with certain other aspects once the statement is admitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I then move to your -- another statement you made on the 18th of September, 2007. MR. DU TOIT: That statement, Mr. Registrar, if you can call it up, please, is 65 ter 05237, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, in front of you is a statement dated the 18th of September, 2007. You also had the opportunity to read that statement and this is the statement that you made on the 18th of September, 2007. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, then I would like to move to another statement that the witness made which I indicated when I -- when you requested me at the beginning, and that is a statement that was allegedly made on the 10th of March, 1996. And as I have indicated, I have given notice to my learned friends and we've loaded this statement already on the e-court. It is not part of the 92 ter submission. I would like permission from the Chamber to add that statement to the 65 ter list and to request the registrar to call it up first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against the document being added to the 65 ter list. I see no objections so therefore permission is granted to add the 10th of March, 1996 statement to the 65 ter list. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, can we then call up, please, 65 ter exhibit 05254, please. That is the statement of March 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, it is in front of you. Can you perhaps just indicate to us this statement that you made on the 10th of March 1996 that you prepared it yourself or that any person assisted you in preparing this statement?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No. I prepared this statement myself on request of the UN. There was no assistance from other individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the statement was basically facts, as I understand it, to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want us to refer to one aspect of the statement, the second-last entry where it reads: "The UNMO team observed several SP policemen being involved in looting of properties." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: I see this statement, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is that in fact a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: The statement I made during that period was, to my belief correct. If I go back now in time, I cannot remember specific details of being special police involved in looting. Now I'm talking about almost 13 years ago and at this moment I cannot recollect anything of these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That I personally observed. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, then lastly, the fourth statement, if I can call it that, is another statement that the witness made during August 1995. It is a similar position like the previous one. I would also like permission to introduce it from the bar table and it has been already loaded on to e-court and the number is 05257, please, and I would also like permission to add that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections against the statement being added to the 65 ter list? No objection. Then permission is granted to add it to the 65 ter list. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, just one aspect regarding this statement that you made in August of 1995, dealing with the loss of certain of your properties. The sort of first paragraph, the fourth line from the bottom you indicate five, 1600 hours, be August, 1995 the HV troops entered Gracac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any troops yourself moving into Gracac on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, not entering Gracac itself. I have seen troops passing by the Jordanian compound from JorBat 3. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I would like to then put some questions to the witness regarding the admissibility of these four statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Steenbergen, as you indicated before, you have basically read these four statements that you just testified about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do the statements accurately reflect the information that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor with the corrections or caveats that you just made?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the information contained in the statements true and correct to the best of your knowledge, subject to the corrections you have made?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you were asked in Court today the same matters here, subject to the caveats, would your information be the same again?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: It would be the same. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, with that I would request that the four statements be moved into evidence and be allocated P numbers. The first one is in the 5236 statement, 18 July 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do understand that you said -- the last two were not part of the 92 ter application you tender them from the bar table. I do understand what you are actually doing is to orally introduce them under Rule 92 ter. MR. DU TOIT: That is so, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I always understand tendered from the bar table just that they are tendered into evidence without any further explanation of a witness, but that is apparently not the case here. Mr. Registrar the first one, 65 ter 5236, statement of the 18th of July 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, P516 is admitted into evidence. Next one is 65 ter 5237, witness statement 18th of September, 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. P517 is admitted into evidence. Next one is 65 ter 5254, statement of the 10th of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P518 in the absence of any objections is admitted into evidence. The last one, 65 ter 5257, statement of the 21st of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P519, in the absence of any objection is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Du Toit. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, as the Court is aware in our 92 ter motion we have also requested to add 16 photographs that's been dealt with in the witness statement of the 18th of September 2007 that has just been admitted as P17 [sic] and I would like to request permission to add also these photographs to the court exhibits and they have been marked as 65 ters 05238 to 05253, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections from what I see, and we learn this from the written submissions as well. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I don't if you want me to read them out one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Let me first see. Yes. Permission to add them to the 65 ter list is granted. May I take it that you want to have them admitted into evidence as well? MR. DU TOIT: Yes, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A practical way of doing it is that Mr. Registrar provides a list and that after the break we'll finally decide on the basis of numbers he will then have provisionally assigned. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would like now to move to read a short witness summary of this pending testimony of this witness and as is the custom I have explained to the witness the purpose of this but maybe the Court will just want to add to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the explanation will do for Mr. Steenbergen. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you. The statement reads as follows: "Witness 147 was an UNMO in Sector South from April until October 1995. During Operation Storm he was deputy team leader of UNMO Team Gracac and a few days later became team leader. "The witness observed the shelling of Gracac on the 4th of August 1995 and coordinated the evacuation of UNMO personnel from the town to the JorBat 3 contingent on that date due to the danger posed by the shelling. "On 5th of August 1995 he observed from JorBat 3 headquarters two groups of HV special police forces advancing towards Gracac. "On the 6th of August 1995 he returned to Gracac and observed and sometimes photographed damage from shelling, looting and burning in and around Gracac in the aftermath of Operation Storm. "In particular, on 6 August 1995, he observed HV special forces being present in Gracac and persons dressed in civilian clothes wearing orange arm bands being involved in an organised way by cleaning and stripping of the houses within Gracac. The persons wearing orange arm bands would remove furniture from houses and place it outside and a mixture of civilian and military trucks would then take it away. "He also observed HV regular troops on the 18th of August 1995 while he was on patrol near Velika Popina on his way to observe many houses on fire but was stopped before reaching his destination by HV regular troops that banged the UNMO vehicle with their weapons. "The witness will also testify that during the end of August 1995 he visited the police station at Gracac to complain about the continuing burning of the houses by the Croatian police. He was informed that it was due to faulty wiring installed by the Serbs." That is the end of the statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Du Toit. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I would like to move now to certain maps that the witness prepared, and I want first, Mr. Registrar, can you please call up 65 ter 04687, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it possible to make a correction from that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This statement is not evidence. It is just to inform the public. If there would be a major mistake of course we would allow you. If is a minor matter then -- but if you think that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there is actually stated Croatian police about the continued burning of houses by Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not observed by me, only being seen houses burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Again, evidence is what is in your statement as corrected by you today. Please proceed. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, is this correct that this is it a map that you prepared and it has been part of your 18 September 2007 statement and you also identified certain areas on this map. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, just maybe for practical purposes we have also prepared another version of this map which we use sort of more computer technology and it's basically similar as this one and we've just added the legend to that so maybe for the purposes may maybe also ask to introduce a second similar map from the bar table and it has been marked exhibit 05271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the markings are -- it is difficult to -- MR. DU TOIT: That is so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have it on the screen then for a second so we can see what the other one looks like. Any objections by the Defence. Not. Then I take it you want to tender them. MR. DU TOIT: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 04687 becomes exhibit number P536. 65 ter 05271 becomes exhibit number P537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P536 and P537 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed. MR. DU TOIT:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, if we can deal with this last map that has been introduced as 537, is it also correct that in your statement you made certain -- identified certain points and just maybe for the sake I don't think that will be in dispute. If I can maybe just read that basically point A on the map deals and you identified the UNMO team offices in the centre of Gracac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then point B on the map is the UNMO team offices in the centre of Gracac as of the -- as of June, July, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And point C on the map is the military storage factory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then points D and point E represent cross-roads. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in our meeting over the weekend I have also requested you to identify the police station that you mentioned in your statement that was admitted. Can you maybe, with the help of Madam Usher on this map just mark it with an F, just identify, please, for us, the location of the police station?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The colour code is known. MR. DU TOIT: Maybe again red if -- if is okay with the, Judge -- with you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, red is for the Prosecution; and blue is for the Defence, yes. MR. DU TOIT: Can you maybe just stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you also identify on this map with a G the place where you stayed in your rented house, as you explained in your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I would like to also move this map into evidence, with the additions of F and G, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P538 is admitted into evidence. And just it avoid whatever misunderstanding, the F on the line going from south to north ending up in a oval just north of the lower circle is F, whereas G refers to the circle lowest on the map marked. Please proceed. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, I would like to move back to the witness statement that the witness made on the 18th July 2007, P16 [sic] please. And specifically to page 3 of that statement, please, paragraph 7 -- sorry, paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, in paragraph 13 of this statement you talked about weapon caches. Do you recall whether you saw any of them in Gracac itself?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, negative. I didn't see any in Gracac itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 14, you also deal with certain aspects in Gracac town specifically. Now, can you remember when you left the town on the 4th of August whether you in fact passed this military storage that is marked C and whether you in fact observed any damage to the storage?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge at this moment. And also we didn't report it during that time. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I see it is 10.30. I don't know, it may be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is an appropriate time for a break. Since the estimates of how much time you would need are not always fully the same, could you give us an indication of how much time you would still need. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I would probably another say 40 minutes, 45 minutes with the witness would suffice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we started at 10.00 with the examination of this witness so it stays even within the most optimistic time estimates. We'll have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du Toit, if you would allow me, I would like to deliver a rather short decision. Mr. Steenbergen, sometimes procedural matters need a minute as well. This is the designation on the Prosecution's application to reply to the Defence responses to the Prosecution's submissions of Rule 92 ter statements of Witness 81. I will now deliver this decision. On the 17th of June, 2008, the Prosecution filed its submission of 92 ter statements for Witness 81. On the 19th of June, the Cermak Defence filed its response, not objecting to the Prosecution's submission. The Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence filed separate responses, objecting to the Prosecution's submission on the 25th of June and 26th of June respectively. Also, on the 26th of June, the Prosecution filed its application to reply to these Defence responses. The Chamber hereby grants the Prosecution leave to file a reply and orders that the Prosecution's reply should be no longer than a thousand words, to be filed no later than 10.00 a.m. on the 1st of July, 2008. The Defence are given leave to respond to the Prosecution's reply and each such response to be no longer than a thousand words and to be filed no longer than close of business on the 2nd of July, 2008. I think the parties were already informally given notice that they should already start working because the time-limits are rather brief. This concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. Mr. Du Toit, please proceed. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, before the break we were looking at your statement, and I'm going to go with it further to just to clarify and to highlight certain passages thereof. MR. DU TOIT: So -- just hold on. If we can move to paragraph 24 of your -- of that statement. I think it is probably the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding paragraph 24 of your statement, can you perhaps just clarify the following for us, please. Did you at any stage in fact observe a shell hitting either one of the houses or your house directly?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe directly a shell. I only observed shrapnel hitting the houses and heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any other aspects or any other sounds while you were standing there at your house?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct. I heard shells flying over my location where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these shells came from?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DU TOIT: Can we move to paragraph 38, please. It's on the next page. Maybe just -- sorry, it's my mistake, to page six because it is in the second part of that paragraph 38, Mr. Registrar. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, at the top of that page, you made the following observation, that you saw or that you stated that there was ten explosions in the general area of Gracac from a direction 220 to 230 degrees. Now can you maybe just explain that, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Actually, that means that the observer hears outgoing fire from that direction, 220 degrees, and if you go to that situation there, it was probably in the vicinity of Mali Alan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the person that observed this, where is this person standing?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That person was at the JorBat 3 compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do I understand you correctly that you observed the 220 to 230 degrees means that they observed shelling from the direction of Mali, as you explained it?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. MR. DU TOIT: If we can go to paragraph 40, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already corrected some aspects thereof. But is it also correct that when we met you also informed me of certain movements of RSK troops that you observed basically on the -- on the 8th -- on the 5th of August, 1995? Can you please just inform the Court about that.

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: What we observed from that location was a group of RSK soldiers passing over a ridge line just north of our location of the JorBat compound, and we could see them travelling in the direction of east south-east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen to that group of people?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shelling directed towards them?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Later on, we seen an incoming, yeah, artillery shell in the vicinity where we first observed this group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the shelling came from?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we move to paragraph 41 of your statement. You talk there about the special police forces that you observed in the morning. Now, can you just explain, did you talk to anybody that -- from these forces that you observed on the 5th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: I cannot recall that it was me or another team member, but I know for sure, or remember the incident that the advancing column in front of JorBat was observed by us and we more or less asked the commander if he wanted to speak to us, and he just briefly came to us and he said, Well, I'm heading for Gracac and I have a job to do and I have no time. I'm in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What language did you speak with you?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: He spoke in clear English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe the clothing that these persons wore that was part of this group when you spoke to the commander?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah. They were wearing olive-green military suits. The commander was wearing a Kevlar helmet and they were wearing ops vests. Not everybody was wearing that same Kevlar helmet. Only I observed that it was the commander who spoke to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to the shoes, did you observe anything?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Regarding the shoes, they were wearing mountain shoes, not the regular army boots but mountain boots. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. Registrar, can we perhaps request to show Exhibit P324 to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, when we met over the weekend, I also showed you this exhibit that was already introduced in court. And do you see the person carrying a television set to the -- to the left of the truck. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I don't think it has ever been established that that is a television set but ... MR. DU TOIT: Okay. I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An object. Please proceed. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the clothes that this person is wearing, if you compare that with the persons that you saw on the 5th of August at the JorBat 3 camp, can you provide any explanation to any similarities, if any?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: This is similar uniform, similar boots, a uniform without camouflage pattern. MR. DU TOIT: And can we just move to the second page of this exhibit, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the person sitting there is also wearing something. You talked previously about them, an ops vest. Do you recognise any similarity here?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I observed the same uniforms as showed in this picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. Registrar, can we go back to the statement again, please. To paragraph 42; page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, the last sentence of that paragraph you indicated that you attempted to travel to the border, you managed to reach Otric but you were turned back by Croatian troops "who were banging our vehicle with their weapons and threatening us." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: This is not correct stated in time. This is later on stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. And we will in fact -- MR. DU TOIT: Sorry, Mr. Registrar, to jump around, but can we show the witness Exhibit D92, page 2, please. And sort of subparagraph 8 where it says UNMO Gracac reported, sort of the last paragraph of that heading, if you can just blow that up for us, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The entry there, Mr. Steenbergen, is as can you see on the 18th of August, 1430 UNMO patrol observed at Velika Popina, and gives the grid reference, approximately 10 burning houses, HV troops at the spot acting in a hostile manner by banging the UNMO vehicle with their weapons. Is this the incident that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the term "HV troops," what do you understand by that or what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: First of all, you can use HV troops as a regular word. It's the same if you go for Dutch troops but you can subdivide them in various types of units or elements. For example, you have general Dutch troops, infantry, or you have Special Forces. And this word can be meant as general, but in this specific incident it is meant as general HV troops, not Special Forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember whether you observed any specific sort of clothes that they were wearing, this group of people that you observed on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I can remember that they wear camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how big was this group of people, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah ... about 20 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that you, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic -- sorry, I apologise, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, counsel, maybe it is a right time just to clear up something, because while we have this document on the screen. The paragraph that you are referring is dated 18th of August, and the paragraph in the middle statement under 42 when he was -- when he was turned back by the Croatian troops is dated around 5th or 6th August. So could you just make clear whether this is referring to that date or some other. Thank you. MR. DU TOIT: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, you heard that and maybe I should have been more clear about that. When you talked about in your statement that around 5th or 6th you receive orders to monitor the movement of HV troops towards and into Bosnia and then we moved into this statement, this sentence that I just read out. What was your intention within you made paragraph 42? Did you want to indicate that also during 5th or 6th August that you visit that place or was it in time distinct from each other, two instances distinct from each other?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yes. It is more in time, because during that period we didn't travel that far outside, and it is more given within the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly when you say 5th or 6th August, you did not mean that you also travelled to that incident on the 5th or the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you were still at the camp?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct, just to finalise this aspect, that you in fact did not go to these incidents of burning houses that you saw because of the incident with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We were, no, we can called it repelled, we were -- this group where we are talking were hitting our vehicles with their rifle-butts, showing hand-grenades, and -- well, made us clear that we were not welcome there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. Registrar, can we go back to the statement again, paragraph 49 on page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, if you read through paragraph 49 and also on 51 and also in 52, you also talk generically about HV troops, if you read paragraph 49, the first line: "Initially we saw regular HV troops taking property from the houses." Now you've already testified to that in the earlier part of your testimony, but can you perhaps just clarify that again for us, please?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I did not observe, at this moment what I can recollect, HV troops doing any looting. What we observed is -- what I remember what happened is that HV troops were present at the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of HV troops were present at the scene?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: During that time I only observed special police forces in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also, in paragraph 39 of your statement, talk about this group of people wearing civilian clothes with an orange band. Can you perhaps just elaborate more on that, please?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah. What we observed was a group of individuals wearing civilian clothes, wearing an orange arm-band. They were stripping houses, taking out furniture, threw it on the street, and later on it was collected by trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you any -- provide any more clarification about the identity of these people? Were they men, women? What were they?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No. What I remember from that period is that were more or less elderly, 50-plus years, not fit for duty. Yeah, just wore civilian clothes with this arm-band and were performing these tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The trucks that you have observed, can you also perhaps be more specific about the trucks that you observed that were used?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Yeah, what we observed during that period as -- were just general and military and civilian trucks, open lorries, where you put, yeah, equipment or just your belongings in the back of the truck. It's open truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to paragraph 58 of your statement. It is the next page, please. You talk of an incident there on the 19th of August, 1995. Were you present when the photographs were taken?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Again, I cannot recollect that I was present during the taking of those pictures I was shown. I can recollect the incident as described in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in, lastly, in paragraph 59, you talk about the visit to -- and you met with Croatian police. Now, the place that you visited, was it the police station?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same one that you previously identified on the map as point F?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you remember what type of clothes that this person wore which you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Now, during that period it was normal civilian -- civilian police in grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you want to go and talk to the police at that stage?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Well, because in -- our houses started burning and we asked for a clarification of -- of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person that you talked to, can you describe him, can you remember who he was or what position he held?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak in English or in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: I don't know at this time anymore, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that -- that the person indicated to you that they would blame the arson on faulty wiring installed by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you observed anything like that before or did you have any information at your disposal at that time that it in fact happened before?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened before? It is unclear to me to what was supposed to have happened or not have happened before. MR. DU TOIT: Sorry, Mr. President, I should be more clear on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that was provided to you that the -- some of the houses in fact was something wrong with the electrical equipment, did you know at that time when you visited that person on the -- round about in August 1995, did you have any other information at your disposal before that, starting, say, from 4th of August, that in fact of the houses that you observed that were burning that there was in fact something wrong with the electrical equipment?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: No, no. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I would like to move now to two further documents that was prepared by this witness, and it is dealt with in 65 ter 00 -- sorry, just one, 05255 and 05256. It is a reports that was prepared by this witness on the 3rd of July, 1995 and as I have indicated also in regard to previous documentation, I have disclosed this to my learned friends but these documents were not filed as part of the 92 ter motion. They came to us -- our knowledge after that, and I just want to -- the witness cannot really talk much about it but I just felt I should of inform the Court ant parties about this document and I would request for it to be added again to the 65 ter list and then moved later into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- two documents mentioned to be included in the 65 ter list. Then grant -- leave is granted to add them to the 65 ter list. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, is it correct that with regard to these two documents, at some stage as part of your duties as an UNMO you were also asked to operate basically as the duty officer at Knin HQ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these two documents were prepared during a week that you were stationed at Knin headquarters and you prepared this information from reports you received from people on the ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally do not have any knowledge of the incidents referred to these two sitreps?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President can I request to move them into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05255 becomes exhibit number P339 -- sorry, P539. 65 ter 05256 becomes exhibit number P540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P539 and P540 are admitted into evidence. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, can you please call up for us 65 ter 00375, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, is it correct that during your meeting over the weekend I also showed you this document, it is a two-page document, allegedly talking about human rights violations within your Team Gracac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the preparation or the information contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: I have not. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, as the Court has probably observed, some of the aspects referred to the witness have already referred to in his statement and I can put it on the record, but I cannot take the matter any further. It was filed as part of the 92 ter motion and, as you just heard, the witness has sort of limited information about the content of this document. But I would, nevertheless, request to move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if there is no basis, I mean the witness is the team leader at that time and I don't know where does this document come from. I mean it just is as a document that is out there. If I doesn't know about it, I mean who does. So on that basis, just as a no foundation, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du Toit. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, as you can see from -- if we can just refer to paragraph 6 of the statement, this is an incident that the bus-stop which is referred to in paragraph 53 of the witness first statement and paragraph 10 of his second statement. Point 8 is an incident, it is it referred to in paragraph 56 of the witness statement, the first statement, and if you can go to the second page, for example, incident number 9, we just talked about it previously, it is also referred to in paragraph 42 of the witness statement. So that is the linkage I could find and maybe for that limited purposes, Mr. President, but as I've indicated it was filed as part of the 65 ter, and as you just heard the witness hasn't got very much information as to the preparation. As you can see at the top right-hand corner it says L 99, this document came -- comes from the statement made by Colonel Leslie before, but that is all can I inform the Court about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say reporting is corroborated or at least consistent with some of the evidence. MR. DU TOIT: Some of the -- that is it all can I say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do the objections stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean I suppose that Your Honour has allowed these documents in before and just takes it to weight. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- stand on ceremony on this particular document. It of course comes in through a witness where we can't cross-examine him because as a team leader he doesn't know anything about it, so I assume Your Honour, if you would admit it, just give it the weight that it is due given the fact that nobody can talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P541.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P541 is admitted into evidence. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, just lastly, as I have indicated before and when you asked me when we -- witness entered the court. We have also prepared a document basically for orientation purposes only and we've loaded it on to the e-court system as 05272. What it basically depicts is a -- using this previous document as a guide and also any other information relevant to Team Gracac which we just dotted down on a map for the assistance basically to the Court and the witness cannot take it any further but we just felt it may be of assistance to the Court in understanding the areas which the witness and other people from Gracac can talk about. So for that limited purposes only, we may offer it as a guide or assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear of any other objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P542 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Du Toit, do we have to understand that we're now talking about a map with all kind of markings. Please proceed with whatever is or may be related to this. MR. DU TOIT: Mr. President, I also prepared, as you can see, from the map, these different locations and I have also linked it back to evidence that is already before court that this witness or other witnesses have given and I have also made a type of an index which I have disclosed to the Defence teams yesterday and we may also be of assistance to the Court in understanding may be relevant evidence that has been introduced regarding these aspects. It is -- as I indicated, it's just an aid to the Court only and I can maybe deal with your staff in assisting you on this aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a table of references rather than anything else, I think. MR. DU TOIT: Yeah, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against -- yes, you're not admitting it. MR. DU TOIT: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not seeking admission but you -- then I should ask whether there is any comment on assisting the Chamber in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the moment, Your Honour, we have no comment, because we have no opportunity to study this map more carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not evidence. What we find here as a matter of fact it is for us and the Defence as well to verify whether these cross-references are accurate or not. Whenever you find any inaccuracy in what we find here, please inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We will notify the Chamber, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the Chamber finds any inaccuracy, we will inform the Defence as well. Please proceed. MR. DU TOIT: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, just before I end, there's just one aspect that I misspoke when I talked about the photographs, and that is I referred to 65 ter 5238 and it should be 5328, so I just apologise for that. But that is all I have for this witness at the moment. Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, as a matter of fact, now we have it on the transcript. Thank you. Thank you Mr. Du Toit. Mr. Mikulicic, are you the first one to cross-examine Mr. Steenbergen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will be the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Steenbergen, Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac and he will be the first to cross-examine you. Could you give us time indications, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me see my clock because this one is obviously not working properly. Well I, believe I could manage by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then for the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I -- counsel is going to cover quite a few bits of territory, I'm not sure how much I have, but it would just be based on exactly what Mr. Mikulicic is going to do. But I don't think it is going to be extensive because I do believe he will cover most of the topics here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: As things stand, Mr. President, we don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. Mr. Mikulicic, you will encouraged to finish today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Steenbergen. My name is Mikulicic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Markac in these proceedings. I'm going to put a few questions to you so could you be so kind as to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Steenbergen, you said that you are a medical officer of the Dutch army and that that is your profession. Before you were send to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, you went through certain training in order to be a military observer of the UN. Could you tell us briefly what the content of this training was and how long it lasted?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Before I was deployed to former Yugoslavia, I received training here in the Netherlands and it lasted about three months. Various trainings throughout the Netherlands. Then we deployed to HQ Zagreb and we received training for about a week there, in-theatre training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The -- did the training involve some basic training and concepts from the field of artillery, including artillery use?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time when you arrived in Zagreb -- or, rather, in May, 1995, when you arrived Gracac, what was your mandate exactly, in rough terms?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: When we arrived at our post in Gracac, our task was to monitor the Zone of Separation between the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that after you became team leader you had between eight and ten men. How many vehicles did your team have at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: There will be -- I cannot exactly recall it, but it will be around three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your assessment, the manpower you had and the vehicles you had, were they sufficient to cover the territory that you had within your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: Given the equipment and related to the task, we felt confident with the equipment we received during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, as you were carrying out your mandate were there any restrictions that were imposed upon you by the authorities of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina or did you have full freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: There were times that we had restrictions of movement and that we were not able to perform or tasks and then we would formally complain with the local military commander and via the HQ of former Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm going back to paragraph 14 of your statement, P516. You said -- this is it paragraph 14, as I said. You described a particular locality and town that you marked as number C in your map and you said that you noticed a truck belonging to the army of the Republic of Serbia Krajina moving there, but you said that you could not be sure as to whether this was a military storage facility or not, because this location was not included in the list that you had received. Did I correctly interpret your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised the statement says trucks. You put to the witness whether it was a truck from -- if we're in paragraph 14, and then the witness says, yes, this reflects what I saw. And now my question of course it was in the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Plural, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not -- at least it was translated you noticed a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. And Mr. -- you were listening to the English. Was it a truck or were there trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would have expected to you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the way in which you carried out your monitoring or observing? On the basis of this, we can deduce that you had a list of localities that you observed on a daily basis or on a weekly basis. Who compiled the list and do you know who did?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: The UNMO Team Gracac team leader decided the patrol route for the specific week, and he also more or less made clear which team with which vehicles was going to drive a specific patrol route. This was done by the team leader. And every morning, this team leader would just clarify the week's mission again and send everybody on his way to do their patrolling. Those patrols were randomly chosen or on indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understood that. But after you arrived in Gracac, according to your statement, you yourself became team leader. In that capacity did you compile lists of facilities and objectives or targets that your team monitored?

utterances.speaker: HERMAN STEENBERGEN
utterances.text: That's not completely correct. I became team leader of UNMO Team Gracac in the third -- approximately the third week of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
